pages.title: Nanomaterials: introduction, classification and synthesis
pages.text:
INTRODUCTION
Nanomaterials are defined as a set of substances where at least one dimension is less than approximately
100nanometers. Nanomaterials are interesting because at the small scale, materials have fundamentally
different properties than at the bulk due to increased surface area to volume ratios.
The behaviour of Nanomaterials may depend more on surface area than particle composition itself.
•         Large spherical particles do not cover much surface area
•         Nanoparticles Equal mass of small platelet particles provides thorough coverage (1 x 106 times more)
Two principal factors cause the properties of Nanomaterials to differ significantly from bulk materials
      •     Increased relative surface area
      •     Quantum Effects
These factors can change or enhance properties such as reactivity, strength and electrical characteristics.

      CLASSIFICTION OF NANOMATERIALS :
    Nanomaterials can have one, two or three dimensions in the nanoscale. Depending on the number of
    dimensions in nanoscale nanomaterials can be classified into various classes.
      Nanomaterials in one dimension:
One dimension is at nanoscale and two dimensions are outside the nanoscale. 1-D nanomaterials exhibit
plate like shape.
Eg. Nanolayers such as thin films and surface coatings, nanoplates and computer chips.
      Nanomaterials in two dimensions:
Two of the dimensions are in the nanoscale and one dimension not confined to nanoscale. This leads to
needle like shaped nanomaterials.
Eg. Nanorods, nanofibers, nanotubes & nanowires (carbon nanotubes and inorganic nanotubes).
   Nanomaterials in three dimensions:
Materials wherein all the dimensions are measured within the nanoscale.
Eg: fullerenes, dendrimers, colloids and quantum dots.

Synthetic Approaches of Nanomaterials:
There are two general approaches to the synthesis of nanomaterials and the fabrication of nanostructures
Top-down approaches– Breaking down matter into more basic building blocks. Frequently uses chemical
or thermal methods.
Bottoms-up approaches – Building complex systems by combining simple atomic- level components.

pages.title: STM: principle and modes
pages.text:
SCANNING TUNNELING MICROSCOPY (STM)
➢ The Scanning Tunnelling Microscope is an electron microscope that develop three- dimensional
  images of the electron cloud around the nucleus.
➢ The STM allows the inspection of the properties of a conductive solid surface at an atomic size.
➢ It is a very important technique in determining the atomic structures and electronic states of the
surface under investigation.

    WORKING PRINCIPLE OF STM
In STM, the sample is scanned by a very fine metallic tip. The tip is mechanically connected to the scanner.
The sharp metal needle is brought close to the surface to be imaged and a bias voltage is applied between
the sample and tip. When voltage is generated between a sample and a tip with a very small distance (a
few angstroms), due to the quantum tunnelling there is an electron transition from the specimen to tip or
from tip to specimen, which corresponds to a tunnel current at the picoamper stage. This tunnelling
current, which occurs when scanning the tip along the specimen surface, is measured and is used to obtain
surface topography, since this current is a function of the distance between the specimen and the tip.




                           Fig 1: Schematic diagram for the working of STM
There are two modes of operation-
Constant height mode:
In this approach the probe-sample distance is fixed. A variation in tunneling current forms the image. This
approaching allows for faster imaging, but only works for flat samples.
Constant current mode:
A constant tunneling current is maintained during scanning.




                                 Fig 2: Different modes of operation in STM

pages.title: STM: advantages, disadvantages and applications
pages.text:
ADVANTAGES
1. STMs are helpful because they can give researchers a three dimensional profile of surface, which allows
   researchers to analysis a multitude of characteristics, including roughness, surface defects and
   determining things about the molecules size and conformation.
2. They will activate in temperatures as low as zero Kelvin up to a few hundred degrees Celsius.
3. Scanning Tunneling Microscope works faster than Atomic Force Microscope.
4. AFM max sample size is 150x150 µm. On the other hand, STM generates mm size length and width.
5. Resolution of STM is much better than AFM.
DISADVANTAGES
1. STM analyses only conductive materials.
2. STM requires very stable and smooth surfaces, excellent vibration control and sharp tips.
3. STMs use highly specialized equipment that is fragile and expensive.
4. STM requires vacuum atmosphere.
5. STM is very specific technique that requires a lot of skill and precision, difficult to use effectively.
APPLICATIONS
1. Scanning tunneling microscopy was developed following the need to obtain local information on
   morphology, structure, etc.
2. STM can be used to “manipulate” objects on the atomic scale with less damage by pushing and
    pulling methods.
3. Using the STM nano-oxidation process single electron transistors (SET) can be fabricated.
4. Growth of metal over another metal i.e., alloy formation is possible.
5. Scanning tunneling microscopy offers the possibility of visualizing biological molecules in
   conditions similar to those in vivo with molecular resolution.

pages.title: AFM: principle and modes
pages.text:
ATOMIC FORCE MICROSCOPY (AFM)
• AFM is a type of scanning probe microscope with demonstrated resolution in the order of
  fractions of a nanometer.
• Determine the roughness of the surface and thickness of a crystal growth layer.
• It can image non-conducting surfaces such as proteins and DNA also.

    WORK PRINCIPLE OF AFM
 AFM provides a 3D profile of the surface on a nanoscale, by measuring forces between a sharp tip (<10
nm) and surface at very short distance (0.2-10 nm tip-sample separation). The tip is supported on a flexible
cantilever. The AFM probe interacts with the substrate through a faster scanning motion. The AFM tip
“gently” touches the surface up/down and side to side motion now the cantilever bends, this bending is
indicative of the tip-sample interaction force. These forces can be monitored through a laser beam reflected
off the cantilever. This reflected laser beam is tracked by a position-sensitive photo-detector (PSPD) that
picks up the vertical and lateral motion of the probe. The deflection sensitivity of these detectors must be
calibrated in terms of how many nanometers of motion correspond to a unit of voltage measured on the
detector.




                           Fig 3: Schematic diagram for the working of AFM
There are 3 primary imaging modes in AFM:
Contact mode : Contact mode operates in the repulsive regime of the van der Waals curve
Tapping mode: Tapping mode is similar to contact mode. In this mode the cantilever is oscillated at
its resonant frequency
Non-contact mode: Non-contact AFM mode uses attractive forces to interact surface with tip.




                             (a)                                 (b)                                 (c)


  Fig 3: Different modes of operation in AFM (a) Contact mode (b) Tapping mode (c) Non contact
                                              mode

pages.title: AFM applications; self-healing materials
pages.text:
ADVANTAGES
1. AFM provides a true three-dimensional surface profile.
2. Samples viewed by AFM do not require any special treatments (such as metal/carbon coatings) that
   would irreversibly change or damage the sample.
3. While an electron microscope needs an expensive vacuum environment for proper operation, most
   AFM modes can work perfectly well in ambient air or even a liquid environment.
4. It possible to study biological macromolecules and even living organisms.


   DISADVANTAGES
1. The AFM can image a maximum height on the order of micrometers and a maximum scanning area
   of around 150 by 150 micrometers
2. Traditionally the AFM could not scan images as fast as SEM, requiring several minutes for a
    typical scan.

   APPLICATIONS
1. The AFM is useful for obtaining three-dimensional topographic information of insulating and
    conducting structures with lateral resolution down to 1.5 nm and vertical resolution down to 0.05 nm.
2. These samples include clusters of atoms and molecules, individual macromolecules, and
   biological species (cells, DNA, proteins).
3. AFM can operate in gas, ambient, and fluid environments and can measure physical properties
   including elasticity, adhesion, hardness, friction and chemical functionality.
4. AFM is useful in tooling studies, roughness measurements and corrosion studies of metals.
5. Polymers: determination of morphology and surface properties, kinetic studies, aging phenomena,
   surface treatment modifications.


SELF-HEALING MATERIALS
Definition:
Self-healing can be defined as the ability of a material to heal (recover/repair) damages
automatically and autonomously, i.e, without any external intervention. Self-healing can be of the
following two types:
    • autonomic (without any intervention);
    • non-autonomic (needs human intervention/external triggering).


Features of self-healing materials:
   ✓   Enhances product safety & durability
   ✓   Leads to longer service life of materials
   ✓   Protects structural bodies
   ✓   Reduction of inefficiency caused by degradation & material failure
   ✓   Reduces inspection & maintenance costs
   ✓   Restores the material performance
   ✓   Sustainable investment approach

pages.title: Self-healing: principle and types
pages.text:
PRINCIPE OF SELF-HEALING MATERIALS:
  This process involves the following steps
  1. Triggering after damage:     The first response is triggering or actuation, which happens almost
  immediately after damage is sustained.
  2. Transportation phase: The second response is transport of materials to the affected area, which also
  happens very quickly.
 3. Chemical repair process: The third response is the chemical repair process. This process differs
    depending on the type of healing mechanism that is in place (e.g., polymerization, entanglement,
    reversible cross-linking).
           These self-healing materials can be classified in three different ways: capsule based, vascular,
and intrinsic. While similar in some ways, these three ways differ in the ways that response is hidden or
prevented until actual damage is sustained.

    Types of self-healing materials:
Intrinsic self -healing materials: It means that the polymer matrix themselves intrinsically have self-
healing properties that can heal after damage occur, although it still need external stimulation.
        So some materials undergo physical or chemical interaction where rearrangements of bonds occur.
Extrinsic self - healing materials: In this condition self -healing material is introduced or pre-embedded
into the polymer matrix.
        Self-healing materials can be further classified as autonomic, where repair is triggered by the
damage itself and non-autonomic where repair is triggered by an external action such as pressure,
radiation, or heat.
         In extrinsic self -healing materials the healing agent is introduced or pre-embedded into the
polymer matrix. Beside encapsulation a self-healing agent could also loaded in pipeline within the matrix.
        When broken (cracked), the mechanical force would destroy the capsule or pipeline and triggers
the release of the healing agent into the damaged zone and self-healing agent would reach the site of
cracking and interact chemically with polymer matrix to close and heal the crack.
        This method allows for the repair of relatively large damaged areas. However, depletion of the
healing agent leads to only a singular healing event. Another extrinsic self-healing system consists of a 3-
dimensional network of capillaries or hollow fibers incorporated into a polymer matrix allow for multiple
healing events.

pages.text:

APPLICATIONS OF SELF-HEALING MATERIALS:
  ❖ Automotive industry: Nissan Motor co. Ltd. has commercialized world´s first self- healing clear
    coat for car surfaces under the trade name: “Scratch Guard Coat“.Paint contains high elastic resins
    that prevent scratches reaching the inner layers of painted car surface effective for 3 years.
    Depending on depth of scratch and temperature in the surrounding environment, the entire
    recovery occurs between 1 and 7 days.
  ❖ Two component polyurethane clear coats from Bayer Material Science under the trade name:
    Desmodur and Desmophen. Coating heals small scratches under the influence of heat (sunlight).
  ❖ Self-healing corrosion resistant coatings beneficial for structural metallic components such as
    steel for achieving long-term service life with reduced maintenance cost.
  ❖ Biocompatible self-healing composite may extend the service life of artificial bone, artificial
    teeth.
  ❖ The very-recent discovery of self-healing rubber may find application in toy industry.
  ❖ Use of composites in aircrafts has grown significantly in the past years. Hollow fibers
    reinforced composites are a possible solution to recover cracking or damage.
  ❖ To maintain colour fastness of garden chairs or window frames during their entire
  ❖ lifetime, polymers with ‘self healing colours’ can be used.
  ❖ Self healing joints in fittings in waterworks or sewer systems that become active at the moment
    a leakage is about to happen.
  ❖ A self healing material just below ski board surface that reacts through the scratch with
    ‘reactive’ oxygen from the air can restore the functionality of the original gliding surface.
  ❖ Self-healing polymers have paved its way in space applications.
  ❖ The construction industry will also find many applications of self-healing materials. For
    example, self-healing concretes may become a reality soon.
  ❖ Polymer/CNTs composites have provided favorable results for self-healing applications in
    storage devices.
  ❖ Currently, innovative self-healing nanosystems are being developed with the help of computer
    simulations for repairing damages.
  ❖ Potential future uses for self-healing plastics include longer lasting cell-phones, cars and laptops,
    whilst larger scale structures will also benefit, from aeroplanes to spacecraft.
  ❖ Oil and gas is a key area. Re-healable products are likely to find uses on platforms - where the
    ability to heal drilling parts would be highly desirable - in pipelines and in refineries.

pages.title: Self-healing applications; biosensors
pages.text:
❖ Developing self-healing coatings, sealants and adhesives based on microcapsule technologies have
     been demonstrated to be able to allow electrical circuits to repair themselves.
   ❖ The technology could be used in the high-performance composite polymer materials replacing metal
     in the new generation of superjumbo aircraft.
   ❖ Self-repairing glass could one day be used in the armored windscreens of military vehicles --
     allowing passengers to drive away from the site of conflict with clear vision -- or in smartphone
     screens.
   ❖ In places that are difficult to access to perform (expensive) repairs, such as at high altitude
     (high buildings, wind turbines at sea), underground (piping) or under the water surface (cables and
     piping).
   ❖ Applications where reliability and safety are key issues, even during overload or unforeseen
     circumstances: airplanes, spacecrafts or long-term storage of nuclear waste.
   ❖ Structures which have to last very long (several decades), such as in large infrastructural applications
     as dikes, dams and tunnels.
   ❖ Applications where large repairs result in a lot of inconvenience in society, such as repairs of
     roads and in energy supply.
   ❖ High-tech equipment to produce high-quality products; machines which must be in operation
     24/7, where downtime should be minimized.
   ❖ Self- healing polymer composites can combat fatigue and to reduce the vane weight in wind
     turbines.
   ❖ In offshore industries – for deep sea research or monitoring of oil and gas wells –there is a need
     for application of self-healing materials called ‘umbilicals. These are complex cables that are
     used for bringing power supply, data signals, hydraulic pressure, or lubrication liquids to and
     from submersed systems.
   ❖ Antifouling coatings which counteracts the fouling process of marine animals.
   ❖ Good protection for High voltage cables at the bottom of the sea.



BIOSENSORS
A biosensor is an analytical device containing an immobilized biological material (enzyme, antibody,
nucleic acid, hormone, organelle, or whole cell) which can specifically interact with an analyte (e.g.
blood, glucose, urea, drug, pesticide) and produce physical, chemical or electrical signals that can be
measured.

Features of biosensor:
   ❖ The device should be tiny & biocompatible.
   ❖ The device should be cheap, easy to use & capable of repeated use.
   ❖ It should be highly specific for the analyte.
   ❖ Assay should be fast, reliable & repeatable.
   ❖ The response should be linear over a useful range of analyte concentrations.
   ❖ Assay cost should be lower than conventional tests.
   ❖ Assay cost should be lower than conventional tests.

pages.title: Biosensor components and characteristics
pages.text:
Components of biosensor
   ➢   Analyte
   ➢   Biological element
   ➢   Transducer
   ➢   Processor
   ➢   Monitor




                               Fig 6: Schematic diagram for Biosensor

Analyte
Substance whose concentration is to be measured. Ex. glucose, urea, drug, pesticide etc.
Biological element
Interacts with the analyte & produces physical, chemical, or electrical signals. Ex. enzyme, antibody,
nucleic acid, hormone, whole cell, organelle.
Transducer
This is the detector element which transforms the signal resulting from the interaction of the analyte with
the biological recognition element into another signal that can be more easily measured and quantified.
Amplifier, microprocessor & display
Biosensor reader device with the associated electronics or signal processors that are primarily responsible
for the display of the results.

CHARACTERISTICS OF BIOSENSORS

1. Selectivity: Selectivity is perhaps the most important feature of a biosensor. Selectivity is the ability of a
   bioreceptor to detect a specific analyte in a sample containing other admixtures and contaminants.
2. Reproducibility: Reproducibility is the ability of the biosensor to generate identical responses for a
   duplicated experimental set-up. The reproducibility is characterised by the precision and accuracy of the
   transducer and electronics in a biosensor.
3. Stability: Stability is the degree of susceptibility to ambient disturbances in and around the biosensing
   system. These disturbances can cause a drift in the output signals of a biosensor under measurement. This
   can cause an error in the measured concentration and can affect the precision and accuracy of the
   biosensor.
4. Sensitivity: The minimum amount of analyte that can be detected by a biosensor defines its limit of
   detection (LOD) or sensitivity. In a number of medical and environmental monitoring applications, a
   biosensor is required to detect analyte concentration of as low as ng/ml or even fg/ml to confirm the
   presence of traces of analytes in a sample.
5. Linearity: Linearity of the biosensor can be associated with the resolution of the biosensor and range of
   analyte concentrations under test. The resolution of the biosensor is defined as the smallest change in the
   concentration of an analyte that is required to bring a change in the response of the biosensor. Depending
   on the application, a good resolution is required as most biosensor applications require not only analyte
   detection but also measurement of concentrations of analyte over a wide working range.

pages.title: Biosensor principle, working and types
pages.text:
PRINCIPLE OF BIOSENSORS:
Biosensors basically involve the quantitative analysis of various substances by converting their
biological actions into measurable signals.




                                  Fig 7: Working principle of biosensor

The biological material is immobilized, and a contact is made between the immobilized biological
material and the transducer.

The analyte binds to the biological material to form a bound analyte which in turn produces the
electronic response that can be measured.

The analyte may sometimes be converted to a product which could be associated with the release
of heat, gas (oxygen), electrons or hydrogen ions.
The transducer then converts the product linked changes into electrical signals which can be amplified and
measured.

WORKING OF BIOSENSORS:
   •   Analyte diffuses from the solution to the surface of the biosensor.
   •   It (analyte) reacts specifically & efficiently with the biological component of the biosensor.
   •   The reaction changes the physicochemical properties of the transducer surface.
   •   This leads to a change in the optical/ electronic properties of the transducer surface.
   •   The change in the optical/electronic properties is measured /converted into electrical signal,
       which is detected.

TYPES OF BIOSENSORS:
Biosensors are classified into two classes:
On the basis of biological element: enzyme biosensor, microbial biosensor, antibody-based
biosensor.
On the basis of sensor device (transducing element), the biosensors are classified as:
   ✓ Electrochemical Biosensors: amperometric, conductometric, potentiometric sensors
   ✓ Calorimetric/Thermal detection Biosensors
   ✓ Optical Biosensors
   ✓ Piezo-electric Biosensors
   ✓ Resonant Biosensors

pages.title: Amperometric biosensors and applications
pages.text:
Electrochemical biosensors are simple devices based on the measurements of electric current, ionic or
conductance changes carried out by bio electrodes. Electrochemical biosensors are classified into three types:
Amperometric Biosensors
Potentiometric Biosensors
Conductimetric Biosensors

Amperometric Biosensors:
These biosensors are based on the movement of electrons (i.e. determination of electric current) as a result of
enzyme-catalysed redox reactions.They measure current(flow of electrons)arising during a reaction.
Clark oxygen electrode which determines reduction of O2, is the simplest form of amperometric biosensor.
Blood-glucose biosensor is a good example of amperometric biosensors, widely used throughout the
world by diabetic patients.
An amperometric biosensor for assessing the freshness of fish has also been developed.

APPLICATIONS OF BIOSENSORS:
Medicine and Health:
Biosensors are successfully used for the quantitative estimation of several biologically important
substances in body fluids e.g. glucose, cholesterol, urea. Glucose biosensor is a boon for diabetic
patients for regular monitoring of blood glucose.
Blood gas monitoring for pH, pCO2 and pO2 is carried out during critical care and surgical monitoring
of patients.
Mutagenicity of several chemicals can be determined by using biosensors.
Several toxic compounds produced in the body can also be detected.
Industry:
Biosensors can be used for monitoring of fermentation products and estimation of various ions. Thus,
biosensors help for improving the fermentation conditions for a better yield.
Now a days, biosensors are employed to measure the odour and freshness of foods. For instance,
freshness of stored fish can be detected by ATPase. ATP is not found in spoiled fish, and this can be
detected by using ATPase.
One pharmaceutical company has developed immobilized cholesterol oxidase system for measurement
of cholesterol concentration in foods (e.g. butter).
Pollution Control:
Biosensors are very helpful to monitor environmental (air, water) pollution.
The concentrations of pesticides and the biological oxygen demand (BOD) can be measured by
biosensors.
Several environmental pollutants can be evaluated for their mutagenicity by employing biosensors.
Applications in Military:
Biosensors have been developed to detect the toxic gases and other chemical agents used during war.

pages.title: Shape-memory alloys: principle
pages.text:
SHAPE MEMORY ALLOYS (SMA)

Shape Memory Alloys are intelligent materials that "remember" their original shape and autonomously
return to it when heated, eliminating the need for external motors or complex mechanisms. They undergo
reversible phase transformations between martensite (low temperature, soft) and austenite (high
temperature, rigid) crystal structures through temperature changes. This unique property enables
compact, energy-efficient actuation without traditional motors, making them ideal for miniaturised
devices and space-constrained applications.
    Examples: NiTiNOL (thermal), NiMnGa, Fe-Pd, Terfenol-D (Magnetic), CuZnSi, CuZnAl,
   CuZnGa, CuZnSn(actuator)
Characteristics of Shape memory alloys:
One-way shape memory effect: (a) Adding a reversible deformation for the one-way effect or severe
deformationwith an irreversible amount for the two-way. (b) heating the sample, (c) and cooling it again
and (d) With the one-way effect, cooling from high temperatures does not cause a macroscopic shape
change. The two-way shape memory effect is the effect that the material remembers two different
shapes: one at low temperatures, and oneat the high temperature shape.




                           Fig 8: One way and two-way shape memory effect
 Principle:
 Shape memory metal alloy can exist in two different temperature dependent crystal structures
 (phases) called Martensite (lower temperature) and Austenite (higher temperature or parent phase).
 Martensite is the relatively soft and easily deformed phase of SMAs which exists at lower
 temperatures.
 Upon deformation this phase takes on second form Austenite. Austenite, the stronger phase of
 SMAs,occurs at higher temperature. Shape of Austenite is cubic.




                                      Fig 9: Shape memory Effect

pages.title: Nitinol: properties and phase transformation
pages.text:
When an external stress is applied to the alloy when it is fully martensitic, the alloy deforms elastically.
If the stress exceeds the martensite yield strength, detwinning occurs and a large non-elastic
deformation will resultuntil the structure is fully detwinned.

The martensite is strain recoverable up to this stage. However, further increase in stress causes the
detwinned structure to deform until the external stress begins to break the atomic bonds between the
martensite layers, resulting in permanent plastic deformation.

For the austenite phase however,it has a higher yield strength compared to martensite. Initially, the
alloy will behave elastically until the stressexceeds its yield strength. From that point onwards, plastic
deformation will ensue causing unrecoverable stretching upon unloading.

Advantages of SMAs
    •   Very high power/weight ratio comparatively
    •   Accessible voltages can accomplish thermo-elastic transformation
    •   Higher strain recovery
    •   Higher strength
    •   Compactness, allowing for reduction in overall actuator size.
    •   Noiseless and silent operation
    •   Higher corrosion resistance
    •   Heat dissipation, need mechanism for cooling
    •   Less stiffness/High flexibility
    •   Relatively expensive to manufacture and machine compared to other materials such as steel and
        aluminium.
    •   Most SMA’s have poor fatigue properties (A steel component may survive for more than one
        hundred timemore cycles than an SMA element).

  Ni–Ti ALLOYS (NITINOL)
    Beuhler discovers shape memory effect in nickel titanium alloy, Nitinol, which proved to be a
    major breakthrough in the field of shape memory alloys. 1970-1980. First reports of nickel-
    titanium implants were used in medical applications. Mid-1990s – Memory metals start to become
    widespread in medicine and soon move to other applications. Ni50Ti50 and the near equiatomic
    Ni–Ti alloys are the best explored system of all shape memory alloys and occupies almost the whole
    market of SMA. Ni–Ti alloys show the best shape memorybehaviour of all SMAs.

  Properties of Nitinol:
    • The Ni-based shape-memory alloys are considered to be engineering materials.
    • These compositions can be manufactured to almost any shape and size.
    • The yield strength of shape-memory alloys is lower than that of conventional steel, but some
      compositionshave a higher yield strength than plastic or aluminium.
    • The yield stress for Ni Ti can reach 500 MPa.
    • The maximum recoverable strain these materials can hold without permanent damage is up to
      8% for somealloys.
    • This compares with a maximum strain 0.5% for conventional steels

Martensite phase: Nitinol wire is easily deformed and holds the new shape when cooled below
transformation temperature.
Energy input triggers the phase transformation, initiating the shape recovery process as material structure
reorganises
Austenite phase: Wire autonomously returns to its original memorised shape, completing the
transformation cycle.

pages.title: Nitinol applications; spectroscopy
pages.text:
Applications of Nitinol:
   • Aircraft: Boeing, General Electric Aircraft Engines, Goodrich Corporation, NASA, and All
     Nippon Airways developed the Variable Geometry Chevron using shape memory alloy that
     reduces aircraft's enginenoise.
   • Robotics: There have also been limited studies on using these materials in robotics (such as
     "Roboterfrau Lara"), as they make it possible to create very light robots. Weak points of the
     technology are energy inefficiency, slow response times, and large hysteresis.
   • Medicine: Shape memory alloys are applied in medicine, for example, as fixation devices for
     osteotomiesin orthopaedic surgery, in dental braces to exert constant tooth‐moving forces on the
     teeth and in stent graftswhere it gives the ability to adapt to the shape of certain blood vessels
     when exposed to body temperature.


SPECTROSCOPY

Spectroscopy is the branch of science dealing with the study of interaction of electromagnetic radiation
with matter like atoms and molecules. The interaction of EMR with matter gives rise to two types of
spectra namely atomic spectra and molecular spectra.

Atomic spectrum arises from the transition of electrons from one energy level to another due to changes
of energy in the atom.

Molecular spectrum involves transition of electrons between rotational and vibrational energy levels in
addition to electronic transition. Therefore molecular spectrum is much more complicated than the atomic
spectrum.

Molecular Spectroscopy provides a clear image of how diatomic and polyatomic molecules interact by
looking at the Frequency, Wavelength, Wave number, Energy, and molecular process also provides most
useful information regarding the shape and size of molecules, the bond angles, bond lengths, strength of
bonds and bond dissociation energies.

Hence molecular spectroscopy is of great use in determining the structure and constitution of compounds.

Spectra

Molecular spectra result from either the absorption or the emission of electromagnetic radiation as
molecules undergo changes from one quantized energy state to another.

The electrons in a molecule possess kinetic energy due to their motions and potential energy arising from
their attraction by the positive nuclei and their mutual repulsion. These two energy factors, along with
the potential energy due to the mutual electrostatic repulsion of the positive nuclei, constitute the
electronic energy of a molecule.

Molecules are not rigid structures, and the motion of the nuclei within the molecular framework gives
rise to vibrational energy levels.

pages.title: UV–Visible: principle and Beer–Lambert law
pages.text:
In the gas phase, where they are widely separated relative to their size, molecules can undergo free
rotation and as a result possess quantized amounts of rotational energy.

In theory, the translational energy of molecules through space is also quantized, but in practice the
quantum effects are so small that they are not observable, and the motion appears continuous.

The interaction of electromagnetic radiation with these molecular energy levels constitutes the basis for
UV-VIS, IR and RAMAN spectroscopy.


UV-VISIBLE SPECTROSCOPY

The UV-Visible range in the electromagnetic spectrum is from 100 – 800nm. The range 100 – 400 nm is
the UV range and from 400 – 800 nm is the Visible range.

When molecules absorb light energy, electrons undergo transitions to higher energy states. These
absorption patterns reveal crucial information about chemical identity and concentration.




                               Fig 10: ES of UV-VIS SPECTROSCOPY


In both UV and Visible Spectroscopy, molecules move to an excited state from the ground state only if
the valence electrons absorb the radiation. It is based on the principle of Beer Lamberts Law.
“When a beam of monochromatic radiation passes through a transparent absorbing medium, the rate
of decrease of intensity of radiation with the thickness of the absorbing medium is proportional to the
intensity of the incident radiation and concentration of the medium”


                                     A = εcl
Where,
         A = absorbance,
         ε = molar absorptivity,
         c = concentration,
         l = path length

Hence, due to the absorption of light, 4 types of transitions are possible. They are:
   1. σ → σ * transition: The energy required for this transition is high (i.e. very short wavelengths;
      150nm). The saturated alkanes will undergo this type of transition.

pages.title: UV–Visible transitions and instrumentation
pages.text:
2.    n → σ * transition: The saturated hydrocarbons attached to hetero atoms will undergo this type
        of transition. Example: Alcohols, amines, ether and water. The energy required for this transition
        is 180-190 nm.

   3.    π → π * transition: The unsaturated hydrocarbons, carbonyl compounds, cyanides and azo
        compounds will undergo this type of transition around 250 nm. Ex: Alkenes, Alkynes, Aldehyde
        and Ketone. The energy required for this transition is very low (i.e. very longer wavelengths).

   4.    n → π * transition: The carbonyl compounds will undergo this type of transition around 275
        nm. Ex: Aldehydes, Ketone and cyanide.




                              Fig 11: Transitions in UV-VIS spectroscopy

INSTRUMENTATION and COMPONENTS:
A spectrophotometer is an instrument which uses monochromatic light. It measures the absorbance of
various solutions at different wavelenths. This instrument scans the entire UV-visible regions.

In a double beam spectrophotometer, radiation from hydrogen lamp or tungsten lamp enters the
monochromator, which produces very narrow band widths.

The beam is then passed through a reference cell and the sample cell by means of rotating mirrors. The
photomultiplier tube is used as a detector which receives alternate pulses of radiation from the reference
and sample beam.

Sources: Commonly used sources of UV radiation are the hydrogen lamp and the deuterium lamp.
Tungsten filament lamp is used for the visible range.
Filters and Monochromators: Tinted glass filters are used to produce monochromatic radiations. Filters
resolve polychromatic light into a relatively wide bandwidth to produce monochromatic radiations.
Monochromator is a device which resolves polychromatic radiation into its individual wavelength and
isolates them into very narrow bands.
 Prism: A prism disperses polychromatic light from a source into its constituent wavelengths. Cornu
quartz and littro prisms are used. Glass prisms are used for visible range while silica, fused silica or
quartz prisms are used for the UV range.
Sample Holder (Cells / Cuvette) : The sample container should be transparent to the UV-visible
radiation. Cuvettes are made ordinary glass or quartz. Fused silica cells are used for the UV range. The
path length of these cuvettes is usually 1 cm.
Solvents: A solvent is selected in such a way that it does not absorb in the UV-visible range. The solvents
that are frequently used are water, methanol, ethanol, hexane, chloroform etc.

pages.title: UV–Visible instrumentation and dye detection
pages.text:
Detectors: The commonly used detectors are photocells, phototubes and photomultiplier tubes.
Amplification and Read out: The transmitted radiation is converted into electrical signal and the
electrical signals are interpreted using ammeters, amplifiers and potentiometers.




                      Fig 12: Schematic Representation of UV-VIS Spectrometer

PRINCIPLE INVOLVED IN UV-VIS SPECTROSCOPY

   ➢ Spectroscopy deals with the interaction of light with matter.
   ➢ Chromophore: It is a covalently unsaturated group which is responsible for absorption of UV
     or visible radiation and may or may not have an impact on the colour to the compound. A
     compound which contains chromophore it is called chromogen. In unsaturated linkage such as
     C=C-,-N=N-, the π electron are loosely bound. These loosely bound electrons required less
     energy for electronic transition and the absorption band occur in near UV region. Example:
     Acetylene possess -C=C- in structure its λmax is 175-180 nm.
   ➢ Auxochrome : It is saturated and unsaturated group which consists of one or more pair of non-
     bonded electron. This group when attached to a Chromophore help in altering the wavelength by
     increasing the intensity of absorption and increases λmax. Examples of Auxochrome are: -OH, -
     NH2, -OR etc.
   ➢ When a substance absorbs light of suitable frequency, there is an increase in the energy of the
     atoms or molecules.
   ➢ Absorption of ultraviolet radiation results in the excitation of electrons from the ground state to a
     higher energy state.
   ➢ Molecules containing π-electrons or non-bonding electrons (n-electrons) can absorb energy
     in the ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum and get excited to higher antibonding
     molecular orbitals (e.g., σ*, π* orbitals).
   ➢ The more easily electrons are excited, the longer the wavelength of light they can absorb.

HOW UV–VIS SPECTROSCOPY DETECTS DYES
Synthetic dyes contain chromophores—functional groups with extended conjugated π-electron systems
that absorb specific wavelengths of visible light. This selective absorption produces characteristic colours
and unique spectral signatures.
Each dye generates a distinctive absorption spectrum that serves as a molecular fingerprint, enabling both
qualitative identification and precise quantitative measurement of concentration in complex
environmental samples.

pages.title: Dyes and methylene blue
pages.text:
DYES
   •  A dye is a colored substance, typically an organic compound, that absorbs and reflects specific
      wavelengths of light, giving it a distinct color.
   • Dyes have an affinity for binding to materials such as textiles, paper, or hair, imparting color
      through chemical or physical interactions.
   • They are widely used in industries such as textiles, cosmetics, and food, and in scientific
      applications like staining in microscopy.
   • In UV–Visible spectroscopy, dyes are studied based on their chromophores, which are
      responsible for absorbing UV or visible light. This absorption commonly involves π → π* or n
      → π* electronic transitions.
   • Approximately 10–15% of dyes used in textile dyeing are discharged into wastewater, leading to
      environmental pollution.
   • Due to their strong chemical stability, dyes are often resistant to natural degradation processes.
   • Many dye pollutants are mutagenic, carcinogenic, and poisonous, posing serious risks to human
      health and aquatic life when released untreated into the environment.
Examples of Dyes
   • Textile Dyes: Methylene Blue (MB), etc.
   • Food Dyes: Tartrazine, Allura Red AC, etc.
   • Cosmetic and Hair Dyes: Para-Phenylenediamine, Henna (Lawsone), etc.
   • Industrial and Specialty Dyes: Rhodamine B, Indigo Carmine, etc.


METHYLENE BLUE: This cationic thiazine dye exhibits strong absorption around 660 nm (red
region), appearing blue to the eye. The intensity at this wavelength enables precise monitoring down to
parts-per-billion concentrations.

Determination of Dye Concentration: Dyes like methylene blue, crystal violet, rhodamine-B show
strong visible absorption peaks.
    ✓ The intensity of absorbance at the dye’s λmax (wavelength of maximum absorption) is directly
        proportional to concentration.
    ✓ Used to monitor: Dye concentration in industrial effluent, & Efficiency of dye removal in
        wastewater treatment.
2. Monitoring Degradation of Dyes
    ✓ During photocatalysis, ozonation, or biological treatment, the dye molecules degrade.
   ✓ UV–Vis spectra show decrease in peak intensity or shift in λmax, indicating:
     Decolorization of dye, Formation of intermediate compounds.




                                 Fig 13: UV-VIS Spectra of MB dye

pages.title: UV–Visible limits; IR principle
pages.text:
Advantages of UV-VIS Spectroscopy
  ✓ Simple, rapid, and inexpensive
  ✓ Non-destructive method
  ✓ Can monitor real-time degradation
  ✓ Suitable for both qualitative and quantitative analysis

Limitations
   ❖ Interference from colored or turbid samples.
   ❖ Requires prior filtration or dilution.
   ❖ Overlapping peaks in mixtures can complicate interpretation.
   ❖ Cannot identify exact chemical structures—only indicates concentration or presence.



IR SPECTROSCOPY IN NIGHT VISION – SECURITY, POLLUTION UNDER
CONTROL – CO SENSOR (PASSIVE INFRARED DETECTION)

   •   Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is based on the absorption of infrared radiation by molecules, causing
       changes in their vibrational and rotational energy levels.
   •   Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is an important analytical tool used to analyze and identify functional
       groups in chemical compounds by examining characteristic molecular vibrations.
   •   It operates by measuring the absorption of infrared radiation, which induces vibrational changes
       within molecules.




                                     Fig 14: InfraRed Spectrum

PRINCIPLE
   •  For a molecular vibration to be IR-active, it must cause a change in dipole moment during the
      vibration.
  • Molecules absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavelengths that correspond to the
      vibrational energy levels of their chemical bonds.
  • This absorption produces a distinctive IR spectrum, which acts as a molecular fingerprint for each
      compound.
Wavelength Range
  • Typically ranges from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹ (wavenumber)
  • Corresponds to 2.5–25 µm in wavelength

pages.title: IR spectrum and molecular vibrations
pages.text:
Main divisions of Infrared Spectrum are:
       Near-IR (0.7–2.5 µm)
       Mid-IR (2.5–25 µm)
       Far-IR (25–1000 µm)
Different molecules absorb IR radiation at characteristic wavelengths, producing an IR spectrum (a
molecular fingerprint).


MODES OF VIBRATIONS:
   •   Molecular vibrations are categorized based on the type of movement of atoms within a molecule.
   •   Primarily, molecular vibrations are classified into two main types.

1. STRETCHING VIBRATIONS
    • Stretching vibrations involve a change in bond length due to elongation or compression of a
      chemical bond.
    • These vibrations are further classified into two types:
a) Symmetric Stretching Vibrations
    • Two or more bonds attached to a central atom stretch in-phase, moving towards or away from the
      central atom simultaneously.
    • Example: In H₂O, both O–H bonds lengthen or shorten together.
b) Asymmetric Stretching Vibrations
    • Two or more bonds attached to a central atom stretch out-of-phase, where one bond lengthens
      while another shortens.
    • Example: In CO₂, one C=O bond lengthens while the other shortens.




                                Fig 15: Different modes of vibration

Stretching vibrations (symmetric and asymmetric) typically appear at higher wavenumbers in IR spectra,
usually in the range of 4000–1500 cm⁻

2. BENDING VIBRATIONS
    • Bending vibrations involve a change in bond angles or the relative positions of atoms without
        significant change in bond length.
    • Bending vibrations are further classified into the following subtypes:
a) Scissoring
    • Two atoms or groups move towards or away from each other in the same plane, similar to the
        blades of scissors.
    • Example: In H₂O, the H–O–H bond angle decreases or increases.

pages.title: IR vibrations; night vision and security
pages.text:
b) Rocking
    • The molecular group moves in-plane, tilting to one side while maintaining the bond angle.
    • Example: In CH₂, the two hydrogen atoms tilt together to one side.
c) Wagging
    • The group moves out-of-plane in a back-and-forth motion towards or away from the molecular
        plane.
    • Example: In CH₂, the hydrogen atoms move up and down relative to the plane.
d) Twisting
    • The group rotates or twists out-of-plane around a bond axis.
    • Example: In ethane, a CH₃ group twists relative to the rest of the molecule.
    • Bending vibrations generally appear at lower wavenumbers (1500–400 cm⁻¹) and require less
        energy than stretching vibrations.
Bending vibrations typically appear at lower wavenumbers (approximately 1500–400 cm⁻¹) and require
less energy than stretching vibrations.

IR SPECTROSCOPY IN NIGHT VISION AND SECURITY
   •   Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is a technique that analyzes the interaction of infrared light with matter
       to identify molecular structures based on vibrational transitions associated with molecules.
   • In night vision and security applications, IR spectroscopy is used to detect and identify objects,
       substances, or activities in low-light or hidden environments by utilizing the unique IR absorption
       or emission signatures of materials.
Principle of IR Spectroscopy in Night Vision and Security
   • Night vision devices detect invisible infrared light, mainly in:
           ➢ Near-infrared (NIR): 0.7–1.4 µm
         ➢ Thermal infrared: 3–14 µm
  • IR spectroscopy enhances night vision by analyzing the unique light patterns or “signatures”
     emitted or reflected by objects based on their chemical composition.
  • Thermal IR cameras detect heat emitted by people, animals, or machines, as temperature
     variations generate characteristic infrared signals.
  • In active night vision, a device emits NIR light, which reflects off objects and returns to a sensor.
  • By studying reflected IR patterns, systems can distinguish between different materials, such as
     living and non-living objects, and even detect specific substances like chemical traces.
  • This capability is crucial for military and security applications, where identifying people, animals,
     or objects in complete darkness is essential.
Mechanism of Detection
  • To identify materials or visualize situations invisible to the human eye, infrared spectrometers or
     cameras measure infrared radiation that is reflected or emitted by objects.
  • In the context of night vision, detection is achieved by sensing thermal infrared radiation or
     reflected infrared light.
  • IR spectroscopy enhances night vision by enabling imaging in low-light conditions and through
     obstructions such as smoke or fog.

pages.title: IR applications; carbon monoxide sensors
pages.text:
REAL-TIME APPLICATIONS OF IR SPECTROSCOPY IN NIGHT VISION AND SECURITY
1. Thermal Imaging for Night Vision
       Thermal cameras based on IR spectroscopy detect mid-infrared (mid-IR) or far-infrared (far-IR)
       radiation (heat) emitted by objects or living beings in complete darkness, such as FLIR systems used
       in security patrols.
2. Surveillance and Perimeter Security
       IR cameras identify intruders or objects based on their heat signatures, even through smoke,
       fog, or camouflage.
       Examples: Border monitoring and surveillance of restricted areas.
3. Detection of Chemicals and Explosives
       IR spectroscopy identifies chemical signatures of explosives or hazardous materials during
       security screening.
       Example: Detection of nitro-based compounds at checkpoints.
4. Gas Leak Detection
       Mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy detects gases such as methane or volatile organic
       compounds (VOCs) in industrial and security environments.
       Useful for pipeline monitoring and preventing potential hazards.
5. Material Identification
       Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy identifies materials like plastics and fabrics during security
       scans.
       Helps detect masked items in airports and border checkpoints.
6. Airport Threat Detection and Screening
       Advanced IR spectroscopy combined with night vision and imaging is used to scan luggage
       and cargo.
       Assists in detecting hazardous materials, explosives, and drugs by identifying their unique IR
       absorption signatures that are often invisible to conventional scanners.
7. Search and Rescue
       Thermal IR imaging locates individuals based on body heat in low-visibility conditions, such
       as nighttime operations or disaster zones.
8. Forensic Analysis
       IR spectroscopy identifies substances such as drugs or residues on surfaces during nighttime
       forensic investigations.

CO SENSORS (CARBON MONOXIDE SENSORS)
  • Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas produced by the incomplete
     combustion of carbon-containing fuels such as gasoline, natural gas, coal, or wood.
  • Common sources of CO include vehicle exhausts, industrial processes, wildfires, and household
     appliances such as heaters and stoves.
  • CO contributes to poor air quality, especially in urban areas with high traffic density or industrial
     activity.
  • It is a primary air pollutant that can persist in the atmosphere for weeks to months, depending on
     environmental conditions.
  • High levels of carbon monoxide (CO) reduce the availability of oxygen in the air by binding
     strongly with hemoglobin, thereby impairing oxygen transport in living organisms.
  • CO affects human health as well as animals, particularly in densely populated regions.
  • CO reacts with other pollutants such as nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) and volatile organic compounds
     (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight to form ground-level ozone, a major component of smog.

pages.title: CO sensing and PUC: source wording
pages.text:
•   Ground-level ozone degrades air quality, harms vegetation, and reduces crop yields by interfering
       with photosynthesis.
   •   Although CO occurs naturally in small amounts, it becomes a serious environmental concern at
       elevated concentrations due to human activities.
   •   Its impacts on air quality, ecosystems, and climate change emphasize the need for effective
       emission control measures.

DETECTION OF CARBON MONOXIDE
    The concentration of CO in air, exhaust systems, or enclosed spaces can be detected and measured
    using CO sensors. CO sensors are essential for Environmental monitoring, Indoor air quality and
    safety monitoring, Industrial safety, Pollution Under Control (PUC) testing for vehicle emissions
    Examples of CO Sensors
        • NDIR (Non-Dispersive Infrared)
        • Electrochemical
        • Semiconductor
        • Colorimetric
        • Photoacoustic


Infrared Spectroscopy in Pollution Under Control (PUC) – CO Sensor
(Passive Infrared Detection)
   •   To detect carbon monoxide (CO) emissions in vehicle exhaust, many Pollution Under Control
       (PUC) systems use infrared (IR) spectroscopy, particularly passive infrared detection.
   •   CO exhibits a strong C=O stretching vibration in the IR region at 4.6–4.7 µm (2143–2170 cm⁻¹).
   •   At this wavelength, CO gas shows strong infrared absorption, enabling precise detection and
       quantification of CO concentration in exhaust samples.

Principle
   •   Passive infrared (PIR) technology detects infrared radiation that is naturally emitted or reflected
       by a substance, eliminating the need for an external IR source such as a laser or LED.
   •   PIR sensors are termed “passive” because they do not emit infrared radiation; instead, they sense
       radiation from external sources.
   •   These sensors are suitable for long-term and continuous monitoring and are energy-efficient.
   •   Common materials used in PIR sensors include:
                   ❖ Lead zirconate titanate (PZT)
                  ❖ Lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃)
                  ❖ Triglycine sulfate (TGS)


Detection of CO Using PIR Sensors
   •   Heated gases such as CO released from motor vehicles naturally emit infrared radiation.
   •   The IR signature of CO is detected by the PIR sensor at CO-specific wavelengths.
   •   The concentration of CO is directly proportional to the intensity of infrared absorption at the
       characteristic CO wavelength (≈ 4.6 µm).

pages.title: PUC working; Raman principle
pages.text:
Working of a PUC System
  • A sample chamber receives exhaust gases from the vehicle.
  • Infrared radiation around 4.6 µm is monitored using a PIR sensor.
  • The CO concentration is determined from the amount of infrared radiation absorbed.
  • Compliance is evaluated by comparing measured values with permissible limits.


Advantages of Passive IR CO Sensing
  1. No active IR source required, resulting in lower power consumption and fewer components.
  2. Highly non-invasive and suitable for remote sensing applications.
  3. Fast response time with real-time monitoring.
  4. High accuracy in CO detection.

Limitations
   1. Ambient temperature and interfering gases (e.g., CO₂, H₂O) may affect readings.
   2. Lower sensitivity compared to active IR systems in some cases.
   3. Still under development for widespread vehicular PUC use and currently more common in remote
      sensing or environmental monitoring.

RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY
   •   Raman spectroscopy is a powerful analytical technique used to study a system’s rotational,
       vibrational, and other low-frequency modes.
   •   It was discovered by Sir C. V. Raman in 1928 and is based on the inelastic scattering of light,
       known as the Raman effect.
   •   When monochromatic light (usually from a laser) interacts with a sample, most of the light is
       elastically scattered.
   •   A very small fraction of light undergoes inelastic scattering, where the energy of the scattered
       light changes due to molecular rotations or vibrations.
   •   This energy shift provides a distinct molecular fingerprint of the sample, useful for structural
       identification.
Raman Effect
   •   Raman scattering refers to the scattering of photons by molecules that are in excited energy states,
       and this phenomenon is called the Raman effect.




                                Fig16: Different scattering mechanism

pages.title: Raman scattering and tumour detection
pages.text:
•   In inelastic scattering, the energy of the scattered photon is different from that of the incident
       photon.
   •   The scattered radiation consists of Stokes and anti-Stokes lines:
             ➢ In Stokes scattering, the scattered photon loses energy.
             ➢ In anti-Stokes scattering, the scattered photon gains energy.
   •   Inelastic scattering occurs due to energy exchange between the incident light and molecular
       vibrations or rotations.

RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY                        IN    DETECTION             OF      TUMOUR           CELLS
(MEDICAL APPLICATIONS)
   •  Raman spectroscopy analyzes the distinct vibrational “fingerprints” of molecules present within
      biological tissues.
   • It provides a non-invasive and label-free technique for tumor identification.
   • The presence of malignant cells can be detected through changes in molecular fingerprints,
      particularly in the composition and structure of biomacromolecules such as proteins, lipids, and
      nucleic acids.
   • By comparing Raman spectra of healthy and malignant tissues, early tumor detection becomes
      possible, aiding in the development of diagnostic tools and potentially guiding surgical
      procedures.
Molecular Changes in Tumors
   • Raman spectroscopy reveals that tumor growth is associated with significant biochemical changes
      in tissues.
   • These changes often include increased protein or lipid levels, which alter the Raman spectral
      signatures.
Raman Imaging and Mapping
   • Raman imaging generates spatial maps that highlight differences in tissue composition.
   • Tumor boundaries can be accurately identified by scanning a laser across tissue samples and
      recording Raman spectra at each location.
   • This technique helps in pinpointing tumor margins, improving precision in diagnosis and
      treatment planning.
Data Processing and Analysis
   • To differentiate between healthy and malignant tissues, Raman spectral data are often processed
      using machine learning algorithms and multivariate analytical methods.
   • Common techniques include Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant
      Analysis (LDA).


WHY USE RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY IN ONCOLOGY??
   ❖ Non-invasive and label-free
   ❖ High chemical specificity
   ❖ Can detect cancer at an early stage
   ❖ Real-time and in vivo analysis
   ❖ Helps surgeons to identify tumour margins

pages.title: Raman applications, advantages and limits
pages.text:
ADVANTAGES
   ❖ Rapid and real-time
   ❖ No sample preparation
   ❖ Minimally invasive
   ❖ High accuracy in tumour identification
   ❖ Can be integrated during surgery

LIMITATIONS
  ❖ Weak signal intensity
  ❖ Requires sensitive detectors
  ❖ Tissue fluorescence may interfere
  ❖ Expensive equipment
  ❖ Requires trained persons


APPLICATIONS OF RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY IN THE DETECTION OF
VARIOUS TUMOUR CELLS
   1. Brain Tumour Detection
         • Helps distinguish between healthy and diseased brain tissue during surgical procedures.
         • Detection is based on nucleic acid signals around 1330 cm⁻¹, aiding in identifying the
             borders of gliomas or glioblastomas.
   2. Breast Cancer Diagnosis
         • Differentiates healthy and malignant breast tissues (e.g., ductal carcinoma).
         • Uses Raman spectral analysis of proteins and lipids in biopsy samples.

   3. Skin Cancer Screening
         • Examines skin lesions for changes in collagen or melanin signatures.
         • Enables non-invasive detection of melanoma or basal cell carcinoma.
   4. Lung Cancer Detection
         • Analyzes sputum or tissue samples to identify lung carcinomas.
         • Detection is based on biochemical changes, such as increased nucleic acid content.
   5. Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
          • Involves analysis of tissue samples to identify cancer-related biochemical changes.
          • Common indicators include elevated nucleic acid levels.
